prize_parts.citation: for the invention of the magic-wavelength optical lattice clock and its development to the 10^-18 level of fractional uncertainty

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: B013 alone, to Katori and Ye. I moved to it from my own opening choice B050 after reading the ballots, and the round-1 exchange has tested that move and I still hold it on the criteria I apply to this prize. The lattice clock is an invention with a clear mechanism: choose the trapping wavelength so the light shift is the same for both clock levels, which removes the Stark and motional shifts while thousands of atoms are interrogated at once. It is an original experiment (Katori's proposal and first strontium lattice clocks) followed by a verified result: 10^-18 level systematic uncertainty at JILA, reproduced and compared at RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, SYRTE and NIST. That independent, quantitative confirmation is the 'absolutely sure' standard I want. It also opens a door to measurements we could not make before: relativistic geodesy, tests of constants and dark-sector couplings, and many-body physics in the clock. The credit separates cleanly into concept and first demonstration (Katori) and record accuracy, stability and the many-body clock (Ye). I note that the chair's observation is correct that part of the support is post-reading convergence, including mine; so I have re-derived my reasons from the criteria and not from the count, and they hold.
statement.case_against: The reservations that remain are real. First, adjacency: the 2005 prize (Hall and Haensch) and the 2012 prize (Wineland, Haroche) cover the comb and the single-ion clock, and the comb is a technical prerequisite for any optical clock. The citation must therefore name the magic-wavelength lattice and the many-atom 10^-18 realisation, and not optical frequency metrology or clocks in general. Second, discovery versus technique: no varying constant or dark-sector signal has come out of the clocks, as Danielsson, Johansson and Lindroth all stress. Third, credit beyond two names: Ludlow, Lemke, Hinkley, Bloom, Takamoto, Lemonde, Hollberg and the Yb and Al+ lineages did important work, and I am recalling priority from memory, not from documents. Fourth, the redefinition of the second is pending. I judge none of these disqualifying, but the credit question is the one I would settle with an expert review before the final ballot.

responses.point: Danielsson says the lattice clock is a triumph of metrology and technique rather than a discovery that changes our picture of nature, and that he is trading discovery value for attribution certainty.
responses.response: I do not think the trade is as stark as you put it. The Physics Prize is for discovery or invention, and the magic-wavelength lattice is an invention that makes a new class of measurement possible, in the same way other instrument-led prizes opened doors to phenomena that could not be seen before. I accept your point that no delivered fundamental-physics result exists yet, and I would not use that argument for the citation. What I would count as sufficient is already in hand: independent laboratories agree at 10^-18 and resolve gravitational redshift over millimetres to centimetres. That is a measured result. If we want to protect against the discovery objection, the citation should say 'invention' and 'development' explicitly and not suggest we are rewarding a discovered constant.

responses.point: Kroll argues that the many-atom statistical gain of the magic-wavelength lattice is something ion clocks cannot offer, so the lattice clock is distinct from the 2012 ion-control prize.
responses.response: I accept that argument for the ion lineage, and I find it the strongest answer to the chair's first question. Where I still press is the comb. Every optical clock relies on the comb as the counter of optical cycles, so the distinction from 2005 rests on the trapping concept and on the demonstrated systematic control, not on frequency measurement. That is why I support a citation that begins with the magic-wavelength lattice clock and puts 10^-18 as the development, and I would avoid your phrasing 'atomic frequency standards', which reads as the general clock field. I also agree with you that the redefinition of the second is a metrological decision, not the discovery, so I would not wait for it.

responses.point: Lindroth supports B013 but asks whether a two-part prize with the ultracold-atom quantum simulation (B001) would be stronger, and she cannot reliably weigh the contributions of Lemonde, Hollberg and others.
responses.response: I considered a two-part prize with B001 and I do not support it. The quantum simulation credit is not settled on our own shortlist: Bloch, Greiner and Esslinger against Zoller and Cirac, and Round 1 shows three different name sets. A second part with an unresolved trio would weaken the clean two-name attribution that is the main strength of B013, and it would not be a scientific improvement, only a larger prize. I share your caution on the early lattice-clock literature. I would ask that the expert review check the 2001-2003 Katori proposals and first demonstrations, and the competing 2000s ideas, so that we are sure the concept is Katori's before we say so in a citation.

responses.point: Eriksson keeps B048 first as a new quantum state, but concedes the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang credit is unrepairable with Zhang deceased and names B013 as the safer fallback.
responses.response: Your concession is the point that decides it for me. You and I agree on what the prize is for: a new state or a new capability, tied to named people who did the original work. For B048 the proposal for the host material and the 2007 measurement involve people who are not on the three-name list, and the 3D work cannot be added under the cap, so I cannot be 'absolutely sure' of the credit. For B013 I can trace proposal, demonstration and verification to two people. I take seriously that you value the stable twenty-year confirmation of B048, and that is a real maturity advantage for that candidate, but it does not repair the attribution. If you move to B013 as your fallback, I would welcome that.

responses.point: Pearce, as Chair, wants expert reviewer input on the relative priority of Katori, Ye and the earlier lattice-clock proposals, and notes that ion-clock, Yb and Al+ groups traded the accuracy record back and forth.
responses.response: I agree an expert review is needed, and I would state its scope: whether Katori's magic-wavelength proposal is the original concept in its 2001-2003 form, whether the first strontium lattice clock demonstrations by his group precede or run parallel to those at JILA, and whether any single contributor (Ludlow, Lemke, Hinkley, Bloom, Takamoto or Lemonde) has a claim that makes two names unfair. On the record trading, I would not base the citation on the 'most accurate clock' wording, because that changes year to year with Al+ and Yb results. A citation built on the invention and the 10^-18 level of uncertainty, which has been independently confirmed, is more durable.

uncertainties: Whether an expert review of the early lattice-clock literature (Katori 2001-2003, Ye, Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and others) leaves Katori and Ye as the right two names; I am working from memory and cannot verify priority.
Whether the committee will accept the citation as distinct from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, which depends on wording around the magic-wavelength lattice.
Whether the absence of a delivered fundamental-physics result, and the pending redefinition of the second, make the timing premature, although I judge the demonstrated 10^-18 performance sufficient.
For my alternatives: B001 has unresolved credit between Bloch, Greiner, Esslinger, Zoller and Cirac, and B050 has attribution between TEM and STEM correctors and a possible cryo-EM novelty issue.
statement.conflict_note: No specific personal or institutional connection to Katori, Ye or B013 is apparent from my profile. Updated disclosure on B050, my alternative: aberration-corrected electron microscopy is my own field, I am President of the International Federation of Societies for Microscopy, and I may know Rose, Haider and Krivanek professionally. I therefore ask that my views on B050 be weighed accordingly and I would recuse myself from any decision centred on B050. Committee colleague Goran Johansson is at Chalmers Physics, and Bernhard Mehlig is in the neighbouring Gothenburg physics environment; neither relationship bears on B013. I recall priority from memory and not from verified documents.
